questiontext.text: Which best describes the core mechanism of merge sort?

answer.text: Divide the array into halves, recursively sort each half, then merge the two sorted halves

feedback.text: Correct — divide, conquer, then combine via merge.

answer.text: Repeatedly swap adjacent out-of-order elements until no swaps remain

feedback.text: That describes bubble sort, not merge sort.

answer.text: Partition around a pivot and recurse on each side

feedback.text: That is quicksort's partitioning, not merging.

answer.text: Build a heap and repeatedly extract the maximum

feedback.text: That is heap sort.

generalfeedback.text: Merge sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm: split, recursively sort, and merge sorted runs.

questiontext.text: What is the worst-case time complexity of merge sort?

feedback.text: Correct — log n levels of merging, each O(n).
Unlike quicksort, merge sort never degrades to quadratic.
Comparison sorts cannot beat O(n log n).
You must at least process every element.

generalfeedback.text: Merge sort's best, average, and worst cases are all O(n log n) — performance is predictable regardless of input order.

questiontext.text: What is the auxiliary space complexity of standard array-based merge sort?

feedback.text: Correct — merging needs a temporary buffer proportional to the input.
Standard merge sort is not in-place; it needs an O(n) buffer.
The recursion stack is O(log n), but the merge buffer dominates at O(n).
Far too much; a single O(n) buffer suffices.

generalfeedback.text: The merge step copies elements into a temporary array of size O(n), so standard merge sort is not in-place.

feedback.text: Correct — a careful merge that favors the left run preserves the order of equal keys.
Merge sort is stable when the merge takes the left element on ties.

questiontext.text: Standard array-based merge sort sorts in place using only O(1) extra memory.

feedback.text: No — the merge step needs an O(n) auxiliary buffer.
Correct — standard merge sort requires O(n) auxiliary space.

questiontext.text: Which statements about merge sort are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: It is well suited to sorting linked lists and forms the basis of external sorting

feedback.text: Yes — linked-list merging needs no random access, and merging drives external sorts.

answer.text: Its running time is O(n log n) regardless of the input's initial order

feedback.text: Yes — best, average, and worst are all O(n log n).

answer.text: It sorts in place with O(1) extra memory

feedback.text: No — standard merge sort needs O(n) auxiliary space.

answer.text: It is unstable, so equal keys may be reordered

feedback.text: No — merge sort is stable.

generalfeedback.text: Merge sort: predictable O(n log n), stable, great for linked lists and external sorting, but needs O(n) extra space.
